title: Mitochondria: The TCA Cycle and Oxidative Phosphorylation
summary: Discover how mitochondria burn fuel completely and turn electron flow into most of the body's ATP.

lessons.title: Pyruvate's Crossroads: Lactate versus Pyruvate Dehydrogenase

levels.kid:
When your body breaks down sugar, it makes a small molecule called **pyruvate**. Pyruvate is like a train that reaches a fork in the tracks.

One track leads into the **mitochondria**, the tiny power plants inside your cells. There, pyruvate gets burned all the way to make lots of energy. But this track needs oxygen.

The other track stays outside, in the main part of the cell. There, pyruvate turns into **lactate**. This track makes only a little energy, but it is very fast, and it works even when oxygen is low.

When you sprint hard, your muscles use the fast lactate track a lot. Later, your liver can turn the lactate back into sugar. Nothing is wasted!
levels.hs:
**Glycolysis** splits one glucose into two molecules of **pyruvate** in the cytoplasm. It makes a little ATP and turns the carrier molecule NAD+ into **NADH**. A cell has only a small supply of NAD+, so it must turn NADH back into NAD+ or glycolysis stops. Pyruvate then has two main fates:

- **Lactate route**: the enzyme **lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)** turns pyruvate into lactate. This uses up NADH and gives back NAD+, so glycolysis can keep running. No oxygen is needed.
- **Aerobic route**: pyruvate enters the mitochondria. There the **pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDH)** removes one carbon as CO2 and makes **acetyl-CoA**, which feeds the next stage of metabolism. This route gives far more ATP in the end, but it depends on oxygen.

Real example: red blood cells have no mitochondria, so they use the lactate route all the time. Sprinting muscles also make a lot of lactate when demand outruns oxygen delivery. Lactate is not simply "waste" that causes soreness. The liver converts it back to glucose in the **Cori cycle**, and the heart can burn lactate as fuel.

Doctors measure blood lactate. High levels can signal that tissues are not getting enough oxygen, for example in shock.
levels.college:
Pyruvate sits at a metabolic branch point. Its fate depends on oxygen, mitochondrial capacity, the cell's energy state and its hormones.

**Lactate dehydrogenase** catalyzes pyruvate + NADH + H+ ⇌ lactate + NAD+. The reaction is near equilibrium and runs in either direction. LDH is a tetramer built from M (LDHA) and H (LDHB) subunits. M-rich forms favor making lactate in muscle; H-rich forms in the heart favor oxidizing lactate back to pyruvate. This reaction regenerates the cytosolic NAD+ needed by glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase.

**Mitochondrial entry**: pyruvate crosses the inner membrane through the **mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC1/MPC2)**. Inside, the **PDH complex** carries out irreversible oxidative decarboxylation: pyruvate + CoA + NAD+ → acetyl-CoA + CO2 + NADH. Three enzymes work together:
- **E1** (pyruvate dehydrogenase) uses **thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP)**
- **E2** (dihydrolipoyl transacetylase) uses **lipoamide** and **CoA**
- **E3** (dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase) uses **FAD** and **NAD+**

The five cofactors come from vitamins: thiamine (B1), riboflavin (B2), niacin (B3), pantothenate (B5), plus lipoic acid.

**Regulation of PDH**:
- Product inhibition by acetyl-CoA and NADH
- **PDH kinase (PDK)** phosphorylates E1 and inactivates it. PDK is activated by acetyl-CoA, NADH and ATP, and inhibited by pyruvate and ADP.
- **PDH phosphatase (PDP)** reactivates the complex. It is stimulated by Ca2+ (important in contracting muscle) and, in fat tissue, by insulin.

Because PDH is irreversible, animals cannot make net glucose from acetyl-CoA. This is why fatty acids are not gluconeogenic. Pyruvate also has other fates: carboxylation to oxaloacetate by **pyruvate carboxylase** (biotin-dependent, activated by acetyl-CoA) and transamination to alanine.
levels.phd:
The partition of pyruvate between LDH and PDH is governed by the cytosolic NADH/NAD+ ratio, MPC flux, and the phosphorylation state of PDH E1α.

**PDH architecture**: mammalian PDH is a giant complex, roughly 9-10 MDa, with an icosahedral core of 60 subunits made of E2 and the E3-binding protein (E3BP), e.g. about 48 E2 + 12 E3BP. E1 (an α2β2 heterotetramer) and E3 dimers attach around this core. Lipoyl domains on flexible linkers swing between active sites, a form of **substrate channeling**. Arsenite and other trivalent arsenicals inactivate the complex by binding the reduced dithiol of lipoamide. E3 is shared with α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and the branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase, so E3 defects affect all three complexes.

**Phosphoregulation**: there are four PDK isoforms that phosphorylate three serines on E1α (Ser293, Ser300 and Ser232; site 1 is dominant). PDK4 is induced by fasting, glucocorticoids and PPARα signaling, which spares glucose during starvation. PDK1 is a HIF-1α target. **Dichloroacetate (DCA)**, a pyruvate analogue, inhibits PDKs and shifts flux toward oxidation.

**The Randle cycle** (1963): oxidizing fatty acids raises mitochondrial acetyl-CoA/CoA and NADH/NAD+ ratios. This inhibits PDH, both directly and through PDK, and reduces glucose oxidation. It is a substrate competition model relevant to insulin resistance.

**Warburg effect**: many tumors make lactate even when oxygen is plentiful (aerobic glycolysis). Drivers include HIF-1α signaling (PDK1, LDHA), MYC, and the M2 isoform of pyruvate kinase. One leading explanation is that NAD+ regeneration and biosynthetic needs, not ATP yield, limit proliferation. Warburg's original idea that tumor mitochondria are defective is now considered largely incorrect.

**Lactate shuttles**: Brooks's cell-to-cell lactate shuttle and the debated astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle (Pellerin and Magistretti, 1994) recast lactate as a fuel and signaling molecule. Monocarboxylate transporters (MCT1-4) move lactate with H+. Isotope tracing (Hui et al., 2017) showed that circulating lactate is a major carbon source for the TCA cycle in most tissues, rivaling glucose.
levels.expert:
**Clinical lactate**: hyperlactatemia is classified as **type A** (tissue hypoxia: shock, ischemia, severe anemia, carbon monoxide) or **type B** (no global hypoxia: liver failure, metformin, thiamine deficiency, malignancy, inborn errors, and epinephrine-driven glycolysis through β2 receptors). In sepsis, much of the lactate is adrenergic and aerobic, not simply hypoxic. The Sepsis-3 criteria (2016) still use lactate in defining septic shock, and lactate clearance tracks prognosis, but treating lactate as a pure marker of oxygen debt is a common pitfall. Hypoperfusion and impaired clearance often coexist.

**Thiamine**: TPP deficiency blocks E1, causing lactic acidosis and Wernicke encephalopathy. Giving glucose to a thiamine-depleted patient (alcohol use disorder, hyperemesis, bariatric surgery) can precipitate Wernicke's. That is why thiamine is given before or with glucose.

**Inborn errors**: **PDH deficiency** is most often caused by mutations in X-linked *PDHA1*, giving lactic acidosis with a normal lactate:pyruvate ratio (about 10-20). By contrast, respiratory chain disease and hypoxia raise the ratio. Brain involvement can include agenesis of the corpus callosum and Leigh syndrome. A **ketogenic diet** bypasses the block by supplying acetyl-CoA from fat and ketones. Some *PDHA1* variants respond to thiamine. Pyruvate carboxylase deficiency is in the differential.

**Neuro-oncology relevance**: in glioblastoma, high LDHA and PDK1 expression reflects HIF signaling in hypoxic tumor regions. Hyperpolarized [1-13C]pyruvate MRI now visualizes the pyruvate-to-lactate conversion in real time in human brain tumors. DCA has been tested in glioblastoma and in congenital lactic acidosis. Its use is limited by peripheral neuropathy, partly linked to slow clearance in GSTZ1 slow metabolizers, and efficacy remains unproven.

**Brain lactate**: brain lactate rises on MR spectroscopy after stroke, in mitochondrial disease (MELAS) and in tumors. Microdialysis lactate/pyruvate ratios guide monitoring in neurocritical care after traumatic brain injury and subarachnoid hemorrhage. A raised ratio with normal oxygen supply suggests mitochondrial dysfunction rather than ischemia.

**Open questions**: how much neurons depend on astrocyte-derived lactate in living animals; whether LDH or MPC inhibitors can be selective for tumors; and lactate's emerging role as a signal through GPR81 (HCAR1) receptors and histone **lactylation** (described in 2019).

keyPoints: Glycolysis makes pyruvate, which goes to lactate (cytosol) or acetyl-CoA (mitochondria)
LDH regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis keeps running without oxygen
PDH irreversibly converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA + CO2 + NADH using 5 cofactors
PDH kinase inactivates PDH; PDH phosphatase (Ca2+, insulin) reactivates it
Thiamine deficiency blocks PDH, causing lactic acidosis and Wernicke encephalopathy
Lactate is a fuel: Cori cycle, heart oxidation, and lactate shuttles

test.q: Why do cells convert pyruvate to lactate when oxygen is scarce?
choices: To release CO2 from the cell
test.explain: LDH oxidizes NADH to NAD+, which glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase needs to keep glycolysis running.

test.q: Where does the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex act?
test.explain: Pyruvate enters the matrix through the MPC, and PDH acts there.

test.q: What are the products of the PDH reaction?
test.explain: PDH carries out oxidative decarboxylation, producing acetyl-CoA, CO2 and NADH.

test.q: Which cofactor does the E1 subunit of PDH use?
test.explain: E1 uses TPP, which comes from vitamin B1. Biotin is used by pyruvate carboxylase instead.

test.q: How does PDH kinase affect the PDH complex?
choices: It adds a lipoyl group to E2
test.explain: PDK phosphorylates E1α and switches the complex off. PDH phosphatase reverses this.

test.q: Which signal stimulates PDH phosphatase in contracting muscle?
test.explain: Ca2+ released during contraction activates PDP, increasing PDH activity when energy demand rises.

test.q: Why can't animals make net glucose from fatty acids?
choices: Fatty acids are blocked from the liver
test.explain: Acetyl-CoA from fat cannot be turned back into pyruvate because the PDH step is irreversible.

test.q: Which cell type relies on the lactate route because it lacks mitochondria?
test.explain: Mature red blood cells have no mitochondria, so they regenerate NAD+ through LDH.

test.q: In the Cori cycle, lactate from muscle is:
choices: Stored as fat in adipose tissue
Converted to glucose by the liver
test.explain: The liver turns lactate back into glucose, which can return to muscle. Red blood cells make lactate rather than oxidize it.

test.q: Which transporter (abbreviation) carries pyruvate across the inner mitochondrial membrane?
test.explain: The mitochondrial pyruvate carrier, made of MPC1 and MPC2, imports pyruvate.

test.q: The enzyme that converts pyruvate to lactate is lactate ___.
test.explain: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) catalyzes this reversible reaction.

test.q: Which vitamin, also called B1, is needed by PDH?
test.explain: Thiamine forms TPP, the E1 cofactor.

kidTest.q: What does your body make when it breaks down sugar?
kidTest.explain: Breaking down sugar makes pyruvate.

kidTest.q: Where does pyruvate get burned to make lots of energy?
kidTest.explain: Mitochondria are the cell's power plants. They break down pyruvate to release large amounts of energy.

kidTest.q: What does the burning track need?
kidTest.explain: Burning pyruvate fully needs oxygen.

kidTest.q: What can the liver do with lactate?
choices: Turn it into new bone tissue
Turn it into keratin for hair
kidTest.explain: The liver recycles lactate into sugar (glucose).

kidTest.q: Hard sprinting makes muscles turn pyruvate into l _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The fast track makes lactate.

advancedTest.q: A child has lactic acidosis with a normal lactate:pyruvate ratio. Which defect is most likely?
advancedTest.explain: PDH deficiency raises both lactate and pyruvate, so the ratio stays normal. Respiratory chain defects and hypoxia raise NADH and increase the ratio.

advancedTest.q: During prolonged fasting, induction of PDK4 mainly serves to:
choices: Increase lactate production for the brain
Spare glucose by limiting pyruvate oxidation
Speed up glucose oxidation in muscle
Activate PDH phosphatase in the liver
advancedTest.explain: PDK4 inactivates PDH, so carbon from pyruvate is conserved for gluconeogenesis while tissues burn fat.

advancedTest.q: Why might dichloroacetate be expected to reduce lactate production in tumors?
choices: It blocks the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier
It inhibits PDK, keeping PDH active
advancedTest.explain: By inhibiting PDK, DCA keeps PDH dephosphorylated and active, shifting pyruvate toward oxidation instead of lactate.

advancedTest.q: In the Randle cycle, high fatty acid oxidation reduces glucose oxidation mainly because:
choices: Pyruvate leaves the cell as alanine
Insulin release is blocked by fatty acids
Rising acetyl-CoA and NADH inhibit PDH
advancedTest.explain: Higher acetyl-CoA/CoA and NADH/NAD+ ratios inhibit PDH directly and by activating PDK.

lessons.title: The Citric Acid Cycle

levels.kid:
Imagine a round factory inside each of your cells. It sits in a tiny power station called the **mitochondrion**. Food pieces come in as little two-carbon bits, like small logs for a fire.

Each log gets added to a carrier that is already waiting. Then the factory turns around in a circle, step by step. At each step, the log gets pulled apart. The carbon leaves as carbon dioxide, the gas you breathe out.

But the best part is what gets saved. The factory catches tiny energy pieces called electrons and loads them onto delivery trucks. The trucks carry the electrons to the next machine, which makes most of your cell's energy.

At the end, the carrier is back where it started, ready for the next log. Round and round it goes!
levels.hs:
The **citric acid cycle** (also called the **Krebs cycle** or **TCA cycle**, for tricarboxylic acid) is a loop of eight chemical reactions in the **mitochondrial matrix**, the inner space of the mitochondrion. It finishes burning the fuel that came from sugars, fats and proteins.

How it works:
- Fuel enters as **acetyl-CoA**, a two-carbon acetyl group attached to a carrier called coenzyme A.
- Acetyl-CoA joins a four-carbon molecule, **oxaloacetate**, to make six-carbon **citrate**.
- Over the next steps, two carbons are removed as **CO2**, and oxaloacetate is regenerated so the loop can run again.

The cycle makes very little ATP directly. Its real job is to collect high-energy electrons. Each turn produces:
- 3 **NADH**
- 1 **FADH2**
- 1 **GTP** (or ATP, depending on the tissue)
- 2 CO2

NADH and FADH2 are electron carriers. They deliver their electrons to the electron transport chain, which makes most of the cell's ATP. Because that chain needs oxygen as the final electron acceptor, the cycle stops when oxygen runs out. It needs no oxygen itself, though, so this is an indirect dependence.

Example: during a long run, fatty acids are broken into many acetyl-CoA molecules, and your muscle mitochondria spin the cycle fast to keep up.

The cycle was worked out by Hans Krebs in 1937, work recognized with the 1953 Nobel Prize.
levels.college:
The TCA cycle oxidizes the acetyl group of acetyl-CoA to two CO2, capturing the released energy as reduced carriers. It runs in the mitochondrial matrix, except succinate dehydrogenase, which is embedded in the inner membrane.

The eight steps:
- **Citrate synthase**: acetyl-CoA + oxaloacetate gives citrate. Thioester hydrolysis makes this step strongly exergonic.
- **Aconitase**: citrate becomes isocitrate via cis-aconitate. The enzyme uses an iron-sulfur cluster.
- **Isocitrate dehydrogenase**: isocitrate gives alpha-ketoglutarate + CO2 + NADH.
- **Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex**: gives succinyl-CoA + CO2 + NADH. Like pyruvate dehydrogenase, it uses TPP, lipoate, CoA, FAD and NAD+.
- **Succinyl-CoA synthetase**: substrate-level phosphorylation produces GTP or ATP.
- **Succinate dehydrogenase**: succinate becomes fumarate. Its FAD is reduced to FADH2. This enzyme is also Complex II of the electron transport chain.
- **Fumarase**: adds water to give malate.
- **Malate dehydrogenase**: malate gives oxaloacetate + NADH. This step has a positive delta G°' (about +30 kJ/mol). It is pulled forward because citrate synthase removes oxaloacetate quickly and keeps its concentration low.

**Yield per acetyl-CoA**: 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 GTP. That totals about 10 ATP equivalents once the carriers are oxidized. Per glucose (2 acetyl-CoA), the cycle accounts for most of the roughly 30-32 ATP.

**Regulation** keeps the cycle matched to energy need. Its main control points are citrate synthase, isocitrate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.
- High **NADH/NAD+** and high **ATP** inhibit these enzymes.
- **Ca2+** activates isocitrate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase. This links the cycle to muscle contraction.
- Succinyl-CoA and citrate act as product inhibitors.

The cycle is **amphibolic**. It serves both catabolism and anabolism, which leads into intermediate draining and refilling.
levels.phd:
The TCA cycle is a catalytic engine. Its intermediates are not consumed in acetyl oxidation, so the flux it can carry depends on the size of the intermediate pool. Biosynthesis drains that pool (**cataplerosis**):
- Citrate is exported for fatty-acid synthesis.
- Alpha-ketoglutarate feeds glutamate production.
- Succinyl-CoA feeds heme synthesis.
- Oxaloacetate feeds gluconeogenesis and aspartate production.

The pool must therefore be refilled (**anaplerosis**). The dominant route is **pyruvate carboxylase**, which converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate and is allosterically activated by acetyl-CoA. Other routes include glutaminolysis to alpha-ketoglutarate, and propionyl-CoA conversion to succinyl-CoA (from odd-chain fatty acids and from valine, isoleucine and methionine). Acetyl-CoA itself cannot achieve net synthesis of intermediates: two carbons enter and two leave as CO2. This is why animals cannot make net glucose from even-chain fatty acids, while plants can, using the glyoxylate shunt (isocitrate lyase and malate synthase).

Stereochemistry gave a classic puzzle. Citrate is prochiral, and aconitase distinguishes its two -CH2COO- arms. Isotope experiments showed asymmetric labeling, which Ogston explained in 1948 with three-point attachment. The CO2 released in a given turn does not derive from the acetyl carbons that just entered; those carbons are lost only in later turns.

The pool is also organized physically. Evidence for **metabolon** formation, meaning substrate channeling between sequential enzymes, has grown through crosslinking and proteomics. Malate dehydrogenase and citrate synthase show electrostatic channeling of oxaloacetate. In vivo, the importance of channeling remains debated.

Control is distributed rather than located at a single step. Flux tracks NADH/NAD+ and ADP status, and the dehydrogenase steps are near-equilibrium sensors of redox state. Mitochondrial Ca2+ entering through the MCU activates three dehydrogenases: PDH via its phosphatase, IDH3 and OGDH. Isocitrate dehydrogenase exists as NAD+-dependent IDH3, which carries cycle flux, and NADP+-dependent IDH2, which supports antioxidant NADPH and reductive carboxylation.

TCA intermediates double as signals:
- Alpha-ketoglutarate is a cosubstrate of about 60 Fe(II)/2OG-dependent dioxygenases, including TET DNA demethylases, JmjC histone demethylases and prolyl hydroxylases that degrade HIF.
- Succinate and fumarate competitively inhibit these enzymes, coupling metabolic state to epigenetics and hypoxic signaling.
levels.expert:
Clinically, the cycle reveals itself through enzyme defects that act as oncogenic or neurological lesions.

**Oncometabolites.** Gain-of-function mutations in IDH1 (R132H) or IDH2 (R140/R172) let the enzyme reduce alpha-ketoglutarate to **D-2-hydroxyglutarate**. This metabolite inhibits TET and histone demethylases, producing a hypermethylator (G-CIMP) phenotype. For a future neurosurgeon, the key point is that IDH mutation now defines WHO CNS5 (2021) diffuse glioma classification: IDH-mutant astrocytoma or 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendroglioma, versus IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, with large prognostic differences.
- 2-HG can be detected noninvasively by MR spectroscopy.
- **Vorasidenib**, a brain-penetrant IDH1/2 inhibitor, prolonged progression-free survival in grade 2 IDH-mutant glioma after surgery (INDIGO trial, FDA approval 2024).
- Ivosidenib and enasidenib are used in AML.

In contrast, loss-of-function mutations in SDH subunits cause paraganglioma and pheochromocytoma, along with GIST and renal cancer. Fumarate hydratase loss causes hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer. In both settings, accumulated succinate or fumarate creates pseudohypoxia; fumarate additionally drives protein succination, including of KEAP1, which activates NRF2. Loss of SDHB staining on immunohistochemistry is a practical screening clue.

**Inborn errors.** Fumarase deficiency and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase deficiency cause encephalopathy. Thiamine deficiency impairs OGDH and PDH, contributing to Wernicke encephalopathy. Glucose given before thiamine can precipitate it in at-risk patients.

**Toxicology.** **Fluoroacetate** (compound 1080) is converted to fluorocitrate. In the classic "lethal synthesis" model, fluorocitrate inhibits aconitase, causing citrate accumulation and cardiac and CNS failure. Arsenite binds the lipoate of OGDH and PDH.

**Research methods and pitfalls.** 13C isotopologue tracing with glucose, glutamine or acetate, analyzed by mass spectrometry or hyperpolarized MRI, reveals pathway use in vivo. These studies show that many tumors, including human gliomas studied intraoperatively, oxidize glucose through the cycle more than the Warburg dogma implied. Interpretation is easy to get wrong:
- Steady state must be confirmed before analysis.
- Label exchange at near-equilibrium steps can mimic net flux.
- Cultured cells, especially in nonphysiological media, often misrepresent tumor metabolism.

Open questions include how much compartmentalized metabolon assembly governs flux, and whether 2-HG lowering will alter the natural history of glioma beyond delaying progression.

keyPoints: The citric acid cycle runs in the mitochondrial matrix and oxidizes acetyl-CoA to 2 CO2
Acetyl-CoA plus oxaloacetate forms citrate; oxaloacetate is regenerated each turn
Each turn yields 3 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 1 GTP
Succinate dehydrogenase is also Complex II of the electron transport chain
Regulated by NADH/NAD+, ATP and Ca2+ at three dehydrogenase-linked steps
Amphibolic: anaplerosis (e.g. pyruvate carboxylase) refills intermediates drained for biosynthesis

test.q: Where in the cell does most of the citric acid cycle take place?
test.explain: The cycle's enzymes are in the matrix, except succinate dehydrogenase, which sits in the inner membrane. Glycolysis, not the TCA cycle, runs in the cytosol.

test.q: Which molecule combines with acetyl-CoA in the first step of the cycle?
test.explain: Citrate synthase joins acetyl-CoA and four-carbon oxaloacetate to make six-carbon citrate.

test.q: How many NADH are produced per turn of the cycle?
test.explain: Isocitrate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and malate dehydrogenase each make one NADH.

test.q: Which cycle enzyme also serves as Complex II of the electron transport chain?
test.explain: Succinate dehydrogenase is bound to the inner mitochondrial membrane and passes electrons from FADH2 into the chain as Complex II. The other dehydrogenases are soluble matrix enzymes that produce NADH.

test.q: The step that makes GTP by substrate-level phosphorylation is catalyzed by:
test.explain: Succinyl-CoA synthetase uses the energy of the thioester bond to make GTP or ATP directly.

test.q: Which change would most directly slow the citric acid cycle?
choices: A high NADH to NAD+ ratio
test.explain: Excess NADH inhibits the regulated dehydrogenases and limits NAD+ for the cycle. Calcium and ADP signal energy demand and speed it up.

test.q: Why does the cycle stop when oxygen is unavailable, even though no step uses oxygen?
choices: CO2 is trapped in the cell without oxygen
NAD+ and FAD are not regenerated
test.explain: The electron transport chain needs oxygen to reoxidize NADH and FADH2. Without it, NAD+ and FAD run out and the dehydrogenases stall.

test.q: Calling the cycle 'amphibolic' means it:
choices: Uses two types of electron carrier
test.explain: The cycle breaks down fuel and also supplies intermediates such as citrate and alpha-ketoglutarate for biosynthesis.

test.q: Malate dehydrogenase has a positive delta G°' yet proceeds forward because:
choices: It is coupled to GTP hydrolysis
Malate is pumped out of the matrix
Oxaloacetate is kept at low concentration
test.explain: Citrate synthase rapidly consumes oxaloacetate, keeping its concentration low and making the actual delta G favorable.

test.q: What is the other common name for the citric acid cycle, honoring the scientist who described it in 1937?
test.explain: Hans Krebs worked out the cycle and shared the 1953 Nobel Prize.

test.q: The six-carbon molecule formed in the first step of the cycle is ___.
test.explain: Citrate gives the cycle its name.

test.q: Refilling cycle intermediates, for example via pyruvate carboxylase, is called ___.
test.explain: Anaplerosis replaces intermediates drained off for biosynthesis (cataplerosis).

kidTest.q: Where in the cell does the round factory work?
kidTest.explain: The cycle runs inside the mitochondrion, the cell's power station.

kidTest.q: What gas leaves the factory when the food bits are pulled apart?
kidTest.explain: The carbon leaves as carbon dioxide, which you breathe out.

kidTest.q: What do the delivery trucks carry?
kidTest.explain: The trucks carry tiny energy pieces called electrons to the next machine, which makes most of the cell's energy.

kidTest.q: Why is it called a cycle?
choices: It uses little wheels to move
It runs mostly during the night
kidTest.explain: The carrier ends where it began, ready for the next turn.

kidTest.q: The cell's tiny power station is called the m _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The mitochondrion is where the round factory works.

advancedTest.q: Why can animals not achieve net glucose synthesis from even-chain fatty acids?
choices: Oxaloacetate is trapped in the matrix during gluconeogenesis
Two acetyl carbons enter and two carbons leave as CO2 each turn
Fatty acid oxidation produces no acetyl-CoA in liver mitochondria
Succinate dehydrogenase is inhibited during fatty acid oxidation
advancedTest.explain: Acetyl-CoA adds no net carbon to the cycle, so oxaloacetate cannot accumulate for gluconeogenesis. Plants bypass this with the glyoxylate shunt.

advancedTest.q: A glioma carries IDH1 R132H. The best mechanistic explanation for its altered epigenome is:
choices: Excess succinyl-CoA directly acetylates the tumor's histones
Accumulated fumarate covalently modifies DNA bases in the tumor
Loss of cycle NADH starves histone acetyltransferases of energy
advancedTest.explain: Mutant IDH makes 2-HG, which competes with alpha-ketoglutarate at TET and JmjC enzymes, producing hypermethylation (G-CIMP).

advancedTest.q: In a 13C tracing study, label appears in an intermediate on the far side of a near-equilibrium step. Why can this mislead?
choices: Mass spectrometry poorly detects labeled intermediates
Carbon-13 is toxic to mitochondrial dehydrogenases
Isotope exchange can occur without net forward flux
Labeled carbons are lost as CO2 before that step
advancedTest.explain: Reversible steps scramble label back and forth, so labeling can reflect exchange rather than net flux through the pathway.

advancedTest.q: Fluoroacetate poisoning raises tissue citrate. The most consistent explanation is:
choices: Fluoroacetate inhibits the pyruvate carboxylase step
Fluorocitrate formed in vivo inhibits aconitase
Fluoroacetate blocks the export of citrate to cytosol
advancedTest.explain: In 'lethal synthesis,' fluoroacetate is converted to fluorocitrate, which blocks aconitase. Citrate then builds up upstream of the block.

lessons.title: The Electron Transport Chain

levels.kid:
Inside almost every cell are tiny power stations called **mitochondria**. They take energy out of food in a clever way.

When your body breaks down food, it grabs tiny bits called **electrons**. Special helper molecules carry these electrons like delivery trucks. They drop them off at a chain of machines stuck in the mitochondria's inner wall.

The electrons get passed from machine to machine, like a ball passed down a line of kids. Each time, a little energy is used to pump tiny particles across the wall. That builds up a push, like water piled up behind a dam.

At the very end, the electrons join the **oxygen** you breathe in, and they make water. That is why you need oxygen to live!
levels.hs:
The **electron transport chain (ETC)** is a series of protein complexes in the **inner mitochondrial membrane**. It is the last stage of cellular respiration.

Earlier steps, like glycolysis and the citric acid cycle, strip high-energy electrons from food. Two **electron carriers** pick them up: **NADH** and **FADH2**. These carriers deliver their electrons to the chain.

The main players:
- **Complex I** accepts electrons from NADH.
- **Complex II** accepts electrons from FADH2 (it is also an enzyme of the citric acid cycle).
- **Ubiquinone** (coenzyme Q), a small fatty molecule, ferries electrons to **Complex III**.
- **Cytochrome c**, a small protein, carries electrons to **Complex IV**.
- Complex IV hands the electrons to **oxygen**, the **final electron acceptor**, forming water.

Electrons move "downhill" in energy, from carriers that hold them loosely to oxygen, which pulls on them strongly. Complexes I, III and IV use the released energy to pump **protons (H+)** from the matrix into the intermembrane space. This creates a **proton gradient**, stored energy that the next lesson's machine, ATP synthase, uses to make ATP.

Real example: cyanide is deadly because it blocks Complex IV. Electrons can no longer reach oxygen, the whole chain backs up, and cells, especially in the brain and heart, quickly run out of energy.
levels.college:
The ETC transfers electrons from NADH and FADH2 to O2 through carriers of increasing **reduction potential (E°')**, coupling the free energy released to proton translocation across the inner membrane.

**The overall drop.** NAD+/NADH has an E°' of about -0.32 V; O2/H2O is about +0.82 V. The difference of ~1.14 V corresponds to a ΔG°' of roughly -220 kJ/mol per NADH (ΔG°' = -nFΔE°', n = 2). Releasing this in steps lets the cell capture it instead of losing it as heat.

**The components:**
- **Complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase).** Contains FMN and a series of iron-sulfur (Fe-S) clusters. It oxidizes NADH, reduces ubiquinone (Q) to ubiquinol (QH2), and pumps 4 H+ per 2 electrons.
- **Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase).** Oxidizes succinate to fumarate via FAD, Fe-S clusters and heme b, and reduces Q. It pumps **no protons**, which is one reason FADH2-derived electrons yield less ATP.
- **Ubiquinone pool.** A lipid-soluble carrier diffusing in the membrane. It also collects electrons from electron-transferring flavoprotein (fatty acid oxidation) and glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase.
- **Complex III (cytochrome bc1).** Transfers electrons from QH2 to cytochrome c via the **Q cycle**, releasing 4 H+ into the intermembrane space per 2 electrons.
- **Cytochrome c.** A water-soluble heme protein in the intermembrane space; it carries one electron at a time.
- **Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase).** Uses hemes a and a3 and copper centers (CuA, CuB) to reduce O2 to 2 H2O, pumping 2 H+ per 2 electrons and consuming matrix protons chemically.

**Totals.** About 10 H+ are pumped per NADH and about 6 per FADH2 (entering at Q). The resulting **proton-motive force** combines a membrane potential (~150-180 mV, matrix negative) and a smaller pH difference.

**Carrier chemistry matters.** Flavins and quinones handle two electrons, or one at a time via semiquinone intermediates. Fe-S clusters and cytochromes carry one. The quinone pool and the Q cycle bridge these two-electron and one-electron steps.
levels.phd:
Mitchell's chemiosmotic hypothesis (1961; Nobel 1978) recast the ETC as a set of vectorial redox-driven proton pumps rather than a source of a high-energy chemical intermediate. Each complex couples electron transfer to proton movement in its own way.

**Complex I** (~45 subunits in mammals, ~1 MDa) is L-shaped. The hydrophilic arm passes electrons from NADH through FMN and a chain of ~8 Fe-S clusters, ending at cluster N2 near a long, narrow quinone-binding tunnel. The membrane arm contains three antiporter-like subunits (ND2, ND4, ND5) plus a fourth pumping module. Cryo-EM structures (Sazanov and others) suggest that quinone reduction drives conformational and electrostatic changes, propagated through a central axis of charged residues, that pump 4 H+ over ~200 Å. Complex I also shows an **active/deactive transition**, which is relevant to ischemia-reperfusion.

**Complex III** works by **Mitchell's Q cycle**. At the Qo site, QH2 oxidation bifurcates: one electron goes to the Rieske Fe-S protein, then cytochrome c1 and cytochrome c, and the other goes through hemes bL and bH to the Qi site. Two Qo turnovers reduce one Q at Qi. Net: 2 cytochrome c reduced, 4 H+ released outward, 2 H+ taken up from the matrix. The Rieske head domain must move ~16-22 Å between sites, a feature exploited by inhibitors. Antimycin acts at Qi and myxothiazol at Qo.

**Complex IV** binds O2 at the heme a3-CuB binuclear center. It moves through peroxy, ferryl and other intermediates without releasing partially reduced oxygen, a key safeguard. Protons travel through the D- and K-channels. Per O2: 4 electrons, 4 "chemical" matrix H+ and 4 pumped H+.

**Supercomplexes.** Blue-native PAGE (Schägger) and later cryo-EM revealed **respirasomes** (I1III2IV1) and III2IV2 assemblies. Whether they speed electron transfer by channeling Q or cytochrome c remains controversial. Kinetic data showing a common, freely diffusing Q pool argue against strict channeling, so supercomplexes may mainly stabilize complexes and limit ROS.

**Thermodynamics in vivo.** The pumping stoichiometry (4/4/2) means that actual ΔG depends on [NADH]/[NAD+], the Q redox state and Δp. Complex I and III operate near equilibrium, which is why high Δp with a reduced Q pool drives **reverse electron transport** through Complex I.
levels.expert:
Clinically, the ETC is where genetics, pharmacology and neurology meet. Mitochondrial disease affects roughly 1 in 4,300 adults, and the brain is disproportionately vulnerable because of its high oxidative demand.

**Dual genome.** Thirteen ETC subunits are encoded by mtDNA (seven in Complex I, cytochrome b in III, three in IV, and two in ATP synthase). Complex II is entirely nuclear-encoded, so isolated Complex II deficiency points to nuclear genes (SDHA-D, SDHAF). Heteroplasmy and threshold effects explain variable, tissue-specific phenotypes and why blood testing can miss mutations found in muscle or urine epithelium.

**Key syndromes for a future neurosurgeon:**
- **Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON)**: m.11778G>A in MT-ND4 (Complex I). It causes subacute painless bilateral vision loss in young men. Idebenone, a short-chain quinone that can bypass Complex I, is approved in Europe, and allotopic ND4 gene therapy trials have shown modest benefit.
- **Leigh syndrome**: symmetric basal ganglia and brainstem lesions on MRI. Over 100 genes are involved, commonly SURF1 (Complex IV assembly) and Complex I subunits.
- **MELAS** (m.3243A>G, tRNA-Leu) gives stroke-like lesions that cross vascular territories. This is a key imaging pitfall that can mimic infarct or tumor.
- **Primary CoQ10 deficiency** (COQ2, COQ8A and others): one of the few treatable forms, responding partially to supplementation.

**Diagnostic pitfalls.** Lactate can be normal between crises, and an elevated lactate:pyruvate ratio supports an ETC defect. Spectrophotometric assays of individual complexes in frozen muscle are sensitive to sample handling. Whole-genome sequencing of nuclear DNA plus mtDNA has largely displaced biopsy-first approaches. FGF21 and GDF15 are emerging serum biomarkers.

**Pharmacology tie-ins.** Metformin's effects were long attributed to Complex I inhibition, but at therapeutic concentrations that link is debated. Alternative proposals include mitochondrial glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase and lysosomal AMPK pathways. Propofol infusion syndrome likely involves ETC and fatty-acid oxidation impairment. Aminoglycoside ototoxicity reflects mitoribosomal susceptibility (m.1555A>G), which in turn reduces ETC subunit synthesis.

**Open questions.** Can hypoxia treat ETC disease? In Ndufs4-knockout mice, chronic hypoxia dramatically extended survival, implying that excess unused O2 is toxic. Researchers are also testing xenotopic bypass enzymes (yeast NDI1, Ciona alternative oxidase) and mitochondrial base editors (DdCBE) for mtDNA correction.

keyPoints: The ETC is a chain of complexes in the inner mitochondrial membrane
NADH feeds Complex I; FADH2 (succinate) feeds Complex II
Ubiquinone and cytochrome c shuttle electrons between complexes
Oxygen is the final electron acceptor and is reduced to water at Complex IV
Complexes I, III and IV pump protons; Complex II pumps none
The proton gradient (proton-motive force) stores energy for ATP synthesis

test.q: Where is the electron transport chain located?

test.q: Which complex receives electrons directly from NADH?

test.q: Which complex pumps no protons?
test.explain: Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) transfers electrons to ubiquinone without pumping protons. This is part of why FADH2 yields less ATP than NADH.

test.q: What is the final electron acceptor of the chain?
test.explain: Complex IV passes electrons to O2, reducing it to water.

test.q: Which carrier is a lipid-soluble molecule that moves within the membrane?
test.explain: Ubiquinone (coenzyme Q) diffuses in the membrane. Cytochrome c is a water-soluble protein in the intermembrane space.

test.q: Cytochrome c carries electrons from:
test.explain: Cytochrome c shuttles single electrons from Complex III (cytochrome bc1) to Complex IV.

test.q: Why do electrons flow from NADH toward oxygen?
choices: Oxygen has a higher reduction potential
Oxygen has a lower reduction potential
NADH is attracted by the membrane charge
test.explain: Electrons move from low (about -0.32 V) to high (about +0.82 V) reduction potential, releasing free energy.

test.q: Cyanide is deadly mainly because it:
choices: Blocks Complex IV and oxygen use
Blocks Complex I and NADH use
test.explain: Cyanide inhibits cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV), so electrons cannot reach oxygen and the chain stops.

test.q: About how many protons are pumped per NADH oxidized?
test.explain: Complex I pumps 4, Complex III 4 and Complex IV 2, giving about 10. FADH2 entering at Q gives about 6.

test.q: Complex III passes electrons to cytochrome c using a mechanism called the Q ___.
test.explain: The Q cycle splits the two electrons of ubiquinol between cytochrome c and the b hemes, releasing 4 H+ outward.

test.q: What gas is reduced to water at the end of the electron transport chain?
test.explain: O2 is the terminal electron acceptor and becomes H2O at Complex IV.

test.q: The stored energy of the proton gradient is called the proton-___ force.
test.explain: The proton-motive force combines the membrane potential and the pH difference across the inner membrane.

kidTest.q: What are mitochondria?
kidTest.explain: Mitochondria turn food energy into energy the cell can use.

kidTest.q: What gets passed down the chain of machines?
kidTest.explain: Electrons are passed from machine to machine, like a ball down a line.

kidTest.q: What do the electrons join at the very end?
kidTest.explain: Electrons join oxygen at the end, and that makes water.

kidTest.q: The pumped particles build up like:
kidTest.explain: The particles pile up on one side, storing energy like water behind a dam.

kidTest.q: Electrons and oxygen make this at the end: w _ _ _ _
kidTest.explain: Oxygen plus electrons (and protons) makes water.

advancedTest.q: Isolated Complex II deficiency most strongly suggests a mutation in:
choices: An mtDNA tRNA gene such as tRNA-Leu
The mtDNA gene for cytochrome b
advancedTest.explain: Complex II is entirely nuclear-encoded, so its isolated deficiency points to nuclear genes like SDHA-D. The other options affect mtDNA-encoded complexes.

advancedTest.q: Why does reverse electron transport through Complex I occur?
choices: High Δp plus reduced Q drive near-equilibrium Complex I backward
Cytochrome c gives electrons back to ubiquinone at the Qi site of III
Complex IV pumps protons back into the matrix when Δp is very high
Oxygen gives up its electrons when the whole chain becomes saturated
advancedTest.explain: Complex I operates close to equilibrium. A large proton-motive force plus a reduced Q pool can push electrons back toward NAD+.

advancedTest.q: Kinetic evidence for a freely diffusing Q pool mainly challenges the idea that supercomplexes:
choices: Exist as stable assemblies in membranes
Help limit the production of reactive oxygen species
Channel quinone directly between partner complexes
Contain Complexes I, III and IV together
advancedTest.explain: A common, diffusing Q pool argues against strict substrate channeling, while still allowing supercomplexes to exist and stabilize complexes.

advancedTest.q: Ndufs4-knockout mice lived longer under chronic hypoxia. The best interpretation is that:
choices: Hypoxia restores Complex I protein synthesis
Excess unused oxygen is toxic when the chain is impaired
Hypoxia raises cytochrome c levels in the brain
Low oxygen makes Complex II begin pumping protons
advancedTest.explain: With Complex I defective, O2 is not consumed and accumulates, likely causing oxidative damage. Lowering O2 removes that toxicity.

lessons.title: ATP Synthase and Chemiosmotic Coupling

levels.kid:
Inside your cells are tiny power stations called **mitochondria**. They pump little charged bits called protons to one side of a wall, like pumping water up behind a dam.

Now the protons really want to flow back. The only door they can use is a special machine called **ATP synthase**. When protons rush through it, part of the machine spins, like a water wheel turning in a river!

Each spin helps snap together a molecule called **ATP**. ATP is the energy coin your body spends to move muscles, think thoughts and keep your heart beating.

So the trick is simple: build up a push, then let it turn a wheel that makes energy coins.
levels.hs:
Your cells make most of their **ATP** (adenosine triphosphate, the cell's energy currency) in mitochondria, using an idea called **chemiosmotic coupling**.

Here's how it works:
- The electron transport chain uses energy from food-derived electrons to pump **protons** (H+ ions) out of the mitochondrial matrix, across the inner membrane, into the space between the two membranes.
- This builds a **proton gradient**: more protons outside than inside, plus an electrical charge difference. Together these store energy, a bit like water held behind a dam.
- The inner membrane is nearly impermeable to protons, so they can return mainly through one enzyme: **ATP synthase**.
- As protons flow back, they make part of ATP synthase physically rotate. The rotation changes the shape of its catalytic sites, which join **ADP** and phosphate into ATP.

This idea was proposed by British biochemist **Peter Mitchell** in 1961. Many scientists doubted him at first, but experiments proved him right, and he won the 1978 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

A key point: making ATP and moving electrons are **coupled**. If ATP synthase stops working, protons pile up, the gradient gets too steep, and the electron transport chain slows down too. That is why oxygen use in mitochondria depends on whether the cell needs more ATP.
levels.college:
**Chemiosmotic coupling** links electron transport to ATP synthesis through an electrochemical proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane.

**The proton-motive force (pmf)** has two parts:
- **Membrane potential (Δψ)**: about 150-180 mV, matrix negative. In mitochondria this is the larger contributor.
- **pH gradient (ΔpH)**: about 0.5-1 unit, matrix more alkaline.
- Total pmf is roughly 180-220 mV, expressed as Δp = Δψ − (2.3RT/F)ΔpH.

**ATP synthase (Complex V)** is an F-type ATPase with two linked motors:
- **F_o**: embedded in the membrane. It has a ring of **c subunits** and an **a subunit** containing two half-channels. Protons enter one half-channel, bind a conserved glutamate on a c subunit, ride the ring nearly a full turn, and exit to the matrix. This drives rotation.
- **F_1**: sits in the matrix, with three α and three β subunits arranged around a central **γ subunit** stalk. Catalysis happens on the β subunits.
- A **peripheral stalk** (stator) holds α3β3 still while γ turns inside it.

**Boyer's binding-change mechanism**: each β subunit cycles through three states, **open (O), loose (L) and tight (T)**. Rotation of the asymmetric γ subunit by 120° shifts each site to the next state. Surprisingly, ATP forms in the tight site with little free-energy change. The energy input from rotation is used mainly to **release** tightly bound ATP.

**Getting substrates in and products out**:
- The **adenine nucleotide translocase (ANT)** swaps matrix ATP⁴⁻ for cytosolic ADP³⁻. Because this is electrogenic, it uses part of Δψ.
- The **phosphate carrier** brings in Pi together with H+, using ΔpH.

**Respiratory control**: when ADP is plentiful, ATP synthase runs, pmf drops and respiration speeds up. When ADP is scarce, pmf builds and electron flow slows. The **P/O ratio**, ATP made per oxygen atom reduced, is about 2.5 for NADH and 1.5 for FADH2-linked substrates.
levels.phd:
**Quantitative energetics.** Synthesizing ATP in the mitochondrial matrix requires roughly +50 kJ/mol under physiological ratios of ATP/ADP·Pi. Each proton crossing at Δp ≈ 200 mV yields about 19 kJ/mol, so at least three protons are needed per ATP. The actual proton cost is set by **c-ring stoichiometry**. A full 360° turn makes 3 ATP (one per β subunit), and it moves n protons, where n is the number of c subunits. Vertebrate mitochondria have **c8 rings** (bovine structure, Watt et al. 2010), giving 8/3 ≈ 2.7 H+ per ATP from F_o. Adding one H+ for phosphate/ATP transport (ANT plus PiC) gives about 3.7 H+ per cytosolic ATP. Combined with 10 H+ pumped per NADH (4 by CI, 4 by CIII, 2 by CIV) and 6 per succinate, this yields P/O values of about 2.7 and 1.6. The textbook values of 2.5 and 1.5 are based on rounding and older assumptions. c-ring sizes vary from c8 to c15 or more across species, a striking example of evolution tuning gear ratios.

**Structural landmarks.** Walker's 1994 bovine F_1 crystal structure showed asymmetric β conformations (β_TP, β_DP, β_E), confirming Boyer's prediction. The two shared the 1997 Nobel Prize. **Noji et al. (1997)** attached a fluorescent actin filament to γ and directly watched unidirectional rotation driven by ATP hydrolysis. Single-molecule work later resolved 120° steps split into roughly 80° (ATP binding) and 40° (hydrolysis/Pi release) substeps. Torque approaches 40 pN·nm, close to 100% thermodynamic efficiency in hydrolysis mode.

**F_o proton path.** The conserved c-subunit glutamate (Glu58 in bovine) is protonated from the intermembrane half-channel. An essential **arginine in subunit a** (Arg159) lowers its pKa at the exit, prevents proton slip and enforces directionality. Rotation is driven by Brownian motion rectified by protonation states and electrostatics.

**Validation of chemiosmosis.** Jagendorf's acid-bath experiment (1966) showed that an imposed pH jump drove ATP synthesis in chloroplasts. The **Racker-Stoeckenius** reconstitution (1974) combined bacteriorhodopsin and ATP synthase in vesicles and produced light-driven ATP without any electron transport chain. This showed the gradient, not a chemical intermediate, is the coupling agent.
levels.expert:
**Supramolecular organization.** In cryo-EM and cryo-tomography (Kühlbrandt and colleagues), mitochondrial ATP synthase forms **dimers** whose roughly 86° angle bends the membrane. Rows of dimers line the highly curved ridges of **cristae**. Subunits e and g, and dimer-specific contacts, are required. Yeast lacking them produce flattened or onion-like cristae. Formation of cristae with ATP synthase rows working with **MICOS** and **OPA1** at cristae junctions may create local proton microdomains, an ongoing debate about whether pmf is uniform across the inner membrane. Live imaging with cristae-resolved potential probes suggests individual cristae can have different membrane potentials.

**Regulation of reverse mode.** When pmf collapses, as in ischemia, F_1F_o runs backward and hydrolyzes ATP to pump protons, draining cellular ATP. **IF1** (ATPase inhibitory factor 1) binds the αβ interface at low matrix pH to block hydrolysis. IF1 levels vary across tissues and are raised in many tumors, linking it to metabolic reprogramming. In neurons and in ischemic brain or heart this reverse mode is clinically relevant, and IF1 is being explored as a target for neuroprotection.

**Human disease.** Mutations in **MT-ATP6** (the mtDNA-encoded subunit a) cause **NARP** (neuropathy, ataxia, retinitis pigmentosa) and maternally inherited **Leigh syndrome**. The classic m.8993T>G variant replaces a conserved leucine near the proton channel. Clinical severity tracks heteroplasmy: higher mutant load leads to Leigh-type necrotizing encephalopathy in the brainstem and basal ganglia. Nuclear assembly factor defects (ATPAF2, TMEM70) cause neonatal lactic acidosis and cardiomyopathy. Diagnostic pitfall: standard spectrophotometric respiratory chain panels may miss Complex V defects unless oligomycin-sensitive ATP hydrolysis or synthesis is specifically assayed.

**The permeability transition pore controversy.** Proposals that ATP synthase dimers or the c-ring form the mPTP, a key mediator of cell death in reperfusion injury, remain contested. Knockouts lacking c-subunits or the peripheral stalk still show a cyclosporin-sensitive permeability transition, so the pore's identity is unresolved.

**Pharmacology angle.** **Bedaquiline**, approved for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, binds the mycobacterial c-ring, a rare example of an ATP synthase drug used clinically. Its selectivity over the human enzyme relies on c-ring sequence differences, an instructive model for targeting bioenergetic machines.

keyPoints: The electron transport chain pumps protons, creating a proton-motive force across the inner membrane
Proton-motive force combines membrane potential (main part) and a pH gradient
Protons return through ATP synthase, spinning the F_o c-ring and the γ stalk
Boyer's binding-change: β sites cycle open, loose, tight; energy mainly releases ATP
Mitchell's chemiosmotic theory (Nobel 1978) explains how electron flow is coupled to ATP synthesis
c-ring size sets protons per ATP; P/O about 2.5 for NADH, 1.5 for FADH2

Brings phosphate in with a proton

lessons.title: Inhibitors, Uncouplers and Reactive Oxygen Species

levels.kid:
Inside your cells are tiny power plants called **mitochondria**. They pass little bits called electrons down a line, like a bucket brigade. The moving buckets pump up a kind of pressure that spins a tiny wheel to make energy.

Some poisons jam the bucket line. **Cyanide** blocks the last helper, so the line stops and cells run out of energy fast.

Other chemicals poke holes in the wall, so the pressure leaks out. The power plant keeps burning food but makes heat instead of energy. Baby animals use this trick on purpose to stay warm!

Sometimes an electron slips off the line and makes a spark called a **free radical**. Cells have cleanup helpers to catch these sparks.
levels.hs:
Mitochondria make most of your ATP using **oxidative phosphorylation**: the **electron transport chain** passes electrons from food-derived carriers to oxygen while pumping protons (H+) across the inner membrane. ATP synthase then lets protons flow back and uses that flow to make ATP. Things can go wrong at three points.

- **Inhibitors** block a step in the chain. Examples: **rotenone** (a plant pesticide) blocks Complex I; **cyanide** and **carbon monoxide** block Complex IV, the enzyme that hands electrons to oxygen. Electron flow stops, so proton pumping and ATP production stop too.
- **Uncouplers** let protons leak back across the membrane without passing through ATP synthase. Fuel is burned and oxygen is used, but the energy becomes **heat** instead of ATP. Brown fat does this naturally with a protein called **UCP1** (thermogenin) to keep newborns warm.
- **Reactive oxygen species (ROS)** form when electrons leak off the chain early and react with oxygen, making **superoxide**. ROS can damage DNA, lipids and proteins. Cells defend with enzymes like **superoxide dismutase** and **catalase**.

A real example: cyanide poisoning from smoke in house fires. Cells have oxygen available but cannot use it, so they switch to anaerobic metabolism and build up **lactic acid**.
levels.college:
Pharmacological tools dissected the respiratory chain because each one acts at a defined site. Their effects on oxygen consumption and ATP synthesis reveal how tightly the two are **coupled**.

**Electron transport inhibitors** (stop both O2 use and ATP synthesis):
- **Complex I**: rotenone, piericidin A. Electrons from succinate (via Complex II) can still enter.
- **Complex II**: malonate (competitive with succinate).
- **Complex III**: antimycin A (Qi site), myxothiazol (Qo site).
- **Complex IV**: cyanide, azide, carbon monoxide, hydrogen sulfide. Cyanide binds ferric heme a3; CO binds the ferrous form.

**ATP synthase inhibitors**: **oligomycin** blocks the Fo proton channel. Because the proton gradient cannot dissipate, it builds until pumping stalls, so O2 consumption also falls. This shows respiration is controlled by ATP demand (**respiratory control**).

**Uncouplers** dissipate the proton-motive force:
- **2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP)** and **FCCP** are lipophilic weak acids that ferry protons across the membrane.
- Oxygen use rises to maximum, ATP synthesis falls, and energy is released as heat, causing hyperthermia.
- **UCP1** in brown adipose tissue is a regulated physiological uncoupler, activated by fatty acids and inhibited by purine nucleotides.

**Reactive oxygen species**: a small fraction of electrons reduce O2 by one electron, mainly at Complex I and Complex III, producing **superoxide (O2•−)**. Superoxide dismutase (MnSOD/SOD2 in the matrix, Cu/ZnSOD/SOD1 in the cytosol) converts it to **H2O2**. Catalase and glutathione peroxidase remove H2O2. Iron can convert H2O2 to the highly reactive **hydroxyl radical** (Fenton reaction).

**Inhibitor vs uncoupler at a glance**: inhibitors lower O2 consumption; uncouplers raise it. Both lower ATP output.
levels.phd:
The canonical way to separate inhibitors from uncouplers is the oxygen-electrode experiment (Chance and Williams' respiratory states). Added ADP drives state 3 respiration and exhausting it returns state 4. Oligomycin produces a state-4-like rate, and FCCP then releases maximal uncoupled respiration. Rotenone and antimycin A abolish the rest. The ratio of state 3 to state 4 is the **respiratory control ratio**. A residual oxygen use in the presence of oligomycin reflects **proton leak**, through the lipid bilayer and through carriers such as ANT and UCPs. Proton leak can account for roughly 20 to 25% of basal metabolic rate in rat hepatocytes and muscle (Rolfe and Brand).

Uncoupler chemistry follows Mitchell's chemiosmotic theory. DNP and FCCP are protonophores: the protonated neutral form crosses the membrane down the gradient, releases H+ in the matrix, and the delocalized anion returns, driven by the membrane potential. UCP1 transports protons using fatty acid anions. Cryo-EM structures (2023) show purine nucleotides binding in the central cavity, locking it in an inhibited conformation.

**Inhibitor topology** maps onto the Q cycle. Antimycin binds the Qi site and myxothiazol and stigmatellin bind Qo. When antimycin is present, semiquinone accumulates at Qo and superoxide production rises markedly toward the intermembrane space.

**ROS site specificity**: at least eleven sites produce superoxide or H2O2 (Brand's catalogue). Two quantitatively dominate: site IQ, driven by **reverse electron transport** when protonmotive force is high and the quinone pool is reduced, and site IIIQo. Reverse transport is blocked by rotenone, which paradoxically lowers ROS from succinate. Superoxide production is steeply dependent on membrane potential, so mild uncoupling reduces it (the hypothesis of "mild uncoupling" for ROS control).

Controversy: the free radical theory of aging (Harman, 1956) predicted antioxidants would extend lifespan. Large trials of antioxidant supplements and many genetic studies failed to support this. ROS, notably H2O2, are now seen as signalling molecules (for example, oxidizing peroxiredoxins and redox-sensitive cysteines in phosphatases), a view summarized as "mitohormesis."
levels.expert:
Clinically, the pattern of mitochondrial toxicity tells you where the block is. Cyanide and hydrogen sulfide poisoning present with severe **lactic acidosis**, collapse and seizures, often with **arterialized venous blood**: tissues fail to extract oxygen, so mixed venous O2 saturation stays high. Pulse oximetry is unreliable in CO poisoning because carboxyhemoglobin reads as oxyhemoglobin, so co-oximetry is required. Hydroxocobalamin, which binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin, is the preferred antidote in smoke inhalation because nitrite-induced methemoglobin would further cut oxygen delivery in patients already loaded with CO.

Uncoupler toxicity is a recognized emergency. DNP, sold illegally as a weight-loss product, causes uncontrollable hyperthermia, tachycardia and rapid rigor, with no specific antidote; management is aggressive cooling and support. Salicylate toxicity includes uncoupling, contributing to fever and metabolic acidosis. Malignant hyperthermia and serotonin toxicity are differentials to keep in mind.

Drug-induced mitochondrial injury is a pharmacology pitfall that standard preclinical screens can miss in glucose-rich media (the **Crabtree effect**: cells make ATP by glycolysis). Swapping glucose for galactose forces reliance on oxidative phosphorylation and unmasks toxicity. Metformin's modest inhibition of Complex I (and effects on mitochondrial glycerophosphate dehydrogenase, still debated) underlies its rare lactic acidosis risk. Linezolid and nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors damage mitochondrial translation or DNA synthesis rather than the chain itself.

Neurosurgical relevance: in **ischemia-reperfusion** injury, succinate accumulates during ischemia and is oxidized on reperfusion, driving a burst of reverse electron transport ROS from Complex I (Chouchani et al., Nature 2014). Malonate prodrugs that block Complex II are being studied to blunt this injury in heart and brain. Rotenone exposure reproduces Parkinson-like dopaminergic neuron loss in rodents, and Complex I deficiency is found in substantia nigra in Parkinson's disease, supporting a mitochondrial link. Mitochondria-targeted antioxidants (MitoQ) and controlled mild uncouplers (such as liver-targeted DNP derivatives in metabolic disease) are open research directions, but none has yet shown clear clinical benefit for neurodegeneration.

keyPoints: Inhibitors block electron flow, lowering both O2 use and ATP synthesis
Rotenone blocks Complex I; antimycin A Complex III; cyanide and CO Complex IV
Oligomycin blocks ATP synthase, and respiration slows because of respiratory control
Uncouplers such as DNP and UCP1 leak protons, raising O2 use and producing heat
Electron leak at Complexes I and III makes superoxide, cleared by SOD, catalase and peroxidases
ROS are both damaging and signalling molecules; antioxidant pills have not reversed aging

test.q: Cyanide stops oxidative phosphorylation by blocking which component?
test.explain: Cyanide binds heme a3 in Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase), the enzyme that hands electrons to oxygen.

test.q: What happens to oxygen consumption when an uncoupler like DNP is added?
test.explain: Uncouplers collapse the proton gradient, so the chain runs at maximum speed and uses more oxygen while ATP synthesis falls.

test.q: Rotenone, a plant pesticide, inhibits which complex?
test.explain: Rotenone blocks Complex I; electrons from succinate can still enter at Complex II.

test.q: Why does oligomycin also reduce oxygen consumption even though it targets ATP synthase?
choices: It binds and blocks cytochrome c
It tears holes in the inner membrane
test.explain: With protons unable to return through ATP synthase, the gradient grows until the chain cannot pump against it. This is respiratory control.

test.q: Brown fat keeps newborns warm using which protein?
test.explain: UCP1 (thermogenin) lets protons leak back, releasing gradient energy as heat.

test.q: Which enzyme converts superoxide into hydrogen peroxide?
test.explain: SOD converts superoxide to H2O2; catalase then breaks H2O2 down to water and oxygen.

test.q: Where in the chain is most superoxide produced?
test.explain: Electron leak to oxygen occurs mainly at Complex I and the Qo site of Complex III.

test.q: A house-fire victim with cyanide poisoning builds up lactic acid because:
choices: Their muscles break down stored protein
Their blood carries too little oxygen
test.explain: Oxygen is present but Complex IV is blocked, so cells switch to anaerobic glycolysis, producing lactate.

test.q: How does DNP carry protons across the inner membrane?
choices: By binding Complex IV heme iron
By pumping protons with ATP energy
By opening the ATP synthase channel
As a lipid-soluble weak acid shuttle
test.explain: DNP is a protonophore: its neutral protonated form crosses the membrane, releases H+, and the anion returns.

test.q: What is the general name for chemicals like DNP that separate electron transport from ATP synthesis?
test.explain: Uncouplers dissipate the proton gradient so energy becomes heat rather than ATP.

test.q: The antibiotic ___ blocks the Fo proton channel of ATP synthase.
test.explain: Oligomycin blocks Fo, stopping ATP synthesis and, through respiratory control, respiration.

test.q: Iron can convert H2O2 into the highly reactive hydroxyl radical in the ___ reaction.
test.explain: The Fenton reaction uses ferrous iron to split H2O2, producing hydroxyl radicals.

kidTest.q: What does cyanide do to a cell's power plant?
kidTest.explain: Cyanide blocks the last helper, so the line stops.

kidTest.q: If the power plant wall leaks, what does it make instead of energy?
kidTest.explain: The leaking pressure turns into heat.

kidTest.q: Who uses the leaky trick on purpose?
kidTest.explain: Babies use brown fat to stay warm this way.

kidTest.q: What is a free radical?
choices: A kind of food that cells eat
A tiny new part grown by cells
A spark from a slipped electron
kidTest.explain: When an electron slips off the line, it makes a damaging spark.

kidTest.q: The tiny power plants in cells are called m _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Mitochondria make most of your cells' energy.

advancedTest.q: Isolated mitochondria respiring on succinate are given rotenone, and superoxide output falls. Best explanation?
choices: Rotenone blocks Complex II and stops succinate oxidation
Rotenone uncouples the membrane and lowers potential
Rotenone blocks reverse electron transport into Complex I
Rotenone directly scavenges superoxide in the matrix
advancedTest.explain: With succinate and high protonmotive force, electrons flow backward into Complex I (site IQ), a major ROS source; rotenone blocks this route.

advancedTest.q: After oligomycin, FCCP is added and respiration jumps to a maximum. What does this show?
choices: FCCP reactivates ATP synthase despite oligomycin
FCCP supplies extra electrons to Complex I
Respiration was limited by the proton gradient, not chain capacity
Oligomycin had irreversibly damaged the electron chain
advancedTest.explain: Collapsing the gradient releases respiratory control, revealing that the chain itself was intact.

advancedTest.q: Why is hydroxocobalamin preferred over nitrites in fire victims with suspected cyanide poisoning?
choices: Hydroxocobalamin removes carbon monoxide from hemoglobin
Nitrites bind Complex I and add a second chain block
Hydroxocobalamin uncouples the chain to restore heat
Nitrites make methemoglobin, worsening oxygen delivery with CO
advancedTest.explain: Methemoglobin lowers oxygen-carrying capacity, dangerous when carboxyhemoglobin is already present.

advancedTest.q: A drug looks harmless to cells in high-glucose medium but toxic in galactose medium. Most likely it:
choices: Inhibits glycolytic enzymes in the cytosol
advancedTest.explain: Galactose forces reliance on oxidative phosphorylation, unmasking mitochondrial toxicity hidden by the Crabtree effect.
